latin.2122: XXVI. Porro hujusmodi decreto subjacere contendunt non tantum bonas causarum liberarum actiones, verum etiam malas: Utrasque enim Deo decernente & volente fieri. Caeterum decretum illud absolutum & energeticum distinguunt in decretum effectivum quo Deus constituit aliquid efficere, & in decretum permissivum quo Deus constituit aliquid permittere. Isti autem Dei decreto effectivo subjiciunt non tantum bonas creaturarum actiones, verum etiam malas, si considerentur in se, & secundum illud quod in iis positivum est, ac prout distinguuntur a malitia quae ipsas denominat. Etenim has & illas fieri existimant Deo non solum decernente, sed etiam causas secundas ciente & movente, & ad hoc aut illud agendum applicante & determinante. Ipsam autem actionum liberarum malitiam a Deo non effici, sed permitti tantum docent.
latin.2123: XXVII. Attamen decretum illud quo malum, qua tale, Deus permittere statuit, licet non effectivum, efficax tamen esse volunt: unde est quod omnia quae fiunt, tam bona quam mala, tribuunt decreto Dei, ut graeca voce vocant, energetico, quod postea subdividunt in effectivum & efficax. Nam juxta ipsos, non minus necesse est ut posito Dei decreto permissivo, malum Deo permittente fiat; quam posito Dei decreto effectivo, necesse est ut fiat bonum Deo probante & efficiente. Adeoque pertendunt vere dici posse & debere non solum quod Deus malum permittere velit, sed etiam quod velit malum fieri ipso permittente: Quia, scilicet, divina voluntas non tantum fertur in mali permissionem, sed etiam in eventum ipsius actionis malae.
latin.2124: XXVIII. Nec tamen inde sequi putant Deum esse peccati autorem: quoniam licet malum Deo decernente fiat, nihilominus non fit Deo efficiente, sed creatura ex certa permissione Dei deficiente. Ac quamvis quod in actione mala positivum est ad Deum ut ad causam efficientem referatur, non tamen propterea Deus mali causa est, quia nempe actionis quantumvis malae entitas est bona, malitia vero formaliter in quadam rectitudinis privatione consistit.
latin.2125: XXIX. Quod si quis objiciat Deum plane videri autorem eorum quae vult esse & fieri, quoniam voluntas Dei est causa rerum, respondent quod aliud est velle rem aliquam per se, aliud velle rem quoad eventum. Deinde quod Deus primo & proprie vult non impedire peccatum: & tantum ex consequenti vult eventum peccati: quia quod Deus non impedit, ideo evenit quia non impedit.
latin.2126: XXX. Ac praeterea distinguunt duplicem Dei voluntatem, unam generalem, alteram specialem. Specialis voluntas ipsis est qua Deus aliquid simul approbat & efficit. Atque voluntatis hujus objectum ab ea pendet, & eam sequitur ut effectus causam. Qua voluntate docent Deum velle bonum, & malum qua malum nolle, juxta illud, Deus non volens iniquitatem es tu. Voluntas vero generalis ex eorum sententia est, qua Deus vult aliquid non esse, vultque etiam certis de causis quaedam non prohibere & consequenter vult evenire, quae tamen simpliciter non probat: sive est decretum Dei, quo vult aliquid non quoad approbationem, & quoad effectionem a se, sed tantum quoad permissam quandam effectionem ab aliis: & sic, inquiunt, res facienda non pendet a voluntate Dei, sed tantum a voluntate deficientis creaturae. Atque hac voluntate dicunt Deum velle peccatum, ut lapsum Adami exempli gratia, non quidem simpliciter, sed solum quia vult illud evenire.
latin.2127: XXXI. Ut vero necessitatem illam, quam Dei decretum quibuslibet eventibus imponit, cum eorum contingentia & libertate concilient, distinguunt primo inter necessitatem absolutam & necessitatem quae est ex hypothesi. Necessitas absoluta est qua simpliciter aliquid aliter esse non potest. Necessitas autem ex hypothesi est, qua quod in se & simpliciter potest non esse, vel aliter esse, posita tamen certa conditione, aliter se habere non potest. Deinde necessitas ab ipsis distinguitur in eam quae est coactionis, & eam quae est tantum infallibilitatis. Necessitas coactionis est, quae per causam extra agentem vim rebus infert, & coacte impellit ut hoc vel illud faciant. Necessitas vero infallibilitatis est, qua res quoad eventum certo & immutabiliter futura est: ita tamen ut si causam rei per se spectemus, possit vel non evenire, vel aliter evenire. Qua de necessitate intelligendum est illud axioma, Omne quod est, dum est, necessario est.
latin.2128: XXXII. His positis distinctionibus, dicunt ea quae fiunt a causis liberis & contingentibus necessario quidem evenire, respectu decreti divini, verum non absolute sed solum ex decreti illius hypothesi; nec eam necessitatem esse coactionis sed tantum infallibilitatis, quia nimirum Deus praeordinavit ut fierent: istud vero necessitatis genus causarum secundarum libertatem non tollere, sed potius stabilire: quoniam videlicet libertas & necessitas non se invicem perimunt, sed libertas & coactio. Nam, inquiunt, ex decreto Dei non tantum necesse est ut causa contingens & libera agat, sed etiam ut agat contingenter & libere: quia Deus decreto suo non solum determinavit singulos rerum eventus, sed etiam eorum modum & rationem.
latin.2129: XXXIII. Quibus addunt, Deum movere causas liberas prout illarum naturae congruum & consentaneum est, nempe voluntatem molliter flectendo, & per objecta ab intellectu monstrata inclinando, nec aliter quam ut homo de eo quod acturus est secum consultet atque deliberet, & ex proprio judicio quod sibi sequendum videatur eligat. Quinimo causam liberam sic a Dei decreto, & quae decretum sequitur motione determinari ad hoc sive istud agendum, ut tamen simul in ea maneat potestas non agendi & aliter agendi, non quidem in sensu composito sed in sensu diviso: quia licet cum divina praeordinatione ad hunc aut illum actum non consistat actus oppositus aut cessatio ab eodem actu, optime tamen cum ea consistit potestas ad actum contrarium, aut ad ipsius actus suspensionem: Quae doctrina est Gulielmi Perkinsi in libello de praedestinationis modo & ordine, & Tuissi illius vindicis, & complurium aliorum clarissimorum apud Reformatos virorum, ut prolixe videre est apud eundem Tuissum toto libro secundo vindiciarum libelli istius Perkinsiani.
latin.2130: XXXIV. Porro quanquam omnium Doctorum istorum virorum suspiciam ingenium & eruditionem, in nulla tamen ex dictis sententiis acquiescere possum. Non enim omnem scrupulum eximunt. Nec eorum ulla est quae non insigni quadam difficultate laborare mihi videatur.
latin.2131: XXXV. Etenim sententia illa quae divinis decretis praestruit scientiam conditionatam de futura inclinatione & propensione voluntatis in hanc vel illam partem, si talis occasio agendi ipsi offeratur; Et quae statuit Deum non aliter praeordinavisse hominum actiones, quam quia voluit illos in eo statu creare, illasque occasiones agendi iis offerre, unde consequi praevidebat illos, mediante ipsius generali concursu, tali modo acturos, & has potius quam illas volitiones elicituros esse non necessitate quadam, vel ab objectis ipsis, vel ab aliqua Dei actione imposita, sed quia ipsi per se sic se essent determinaturi, cum contrarium esset in eorum potestate: haec, inquam, sententia multa quidem incommoda vitat quibus urgentur aliae sententiae: sed cum ea difficulter conciliari potest gratia victrix & per se efficax, quae liberum sibi subjicit arbitrium, minime vero libero arbitrio subjicienda est, quam praedicat Schola orthodoxa.
latin.2132: XXXVI. Adde quod, etsi Deus, priusquam aliquid de nobis decernat, praesciat quid voluntas factura sit, ex hypothesi quod constituatur in talibus circumstantiis, & ejusmodi motiva accedant; tamen si Deus aliquid simpliciter futurum praefinit, ante praevisam absolute voluntatis nostrae determinationem, inde nascitur quaedam necessitas antecedens, quandoquidem quod Deus praedefinit omnino necesse est fore: quae necessitas non minus libertati repugnare videtur, quam si nulla talis scientia conditionata praecessisset, cum scientia ista non faciat ut tale Dei decretum sit in nostra potestate.
latin.2133: XXXVII. In sententia Joan. Strangii illud omnino mihi videtur improbabile, quod inter eas quae ab hominibus consulto & deliberate fiunt, discrimen quoad libertatem statuit; quasi quaedam duntaxat liberae essent ea libertate quae sita est in indifferentia, & per quam homo potest agere vel non agere; hoc vel illud agere, aliae vero solum libertate simplici ad quam non requiritur voluntatis indeterminatio, sed tantum ut homo sponte & cum judicio agat. Ad quod genus pertinere putat, non solum omnes actiones bonas, sed etiam multas quae ex suo genere nec bonae, nec malae sunt. Cum enim experiamur nos eodem modo uti ratione & judicio nostro, ac eligendi potestate, non tantum in omnibus vitae civilis actionibus, sed etiam in bonis, quare putabimus alias aliis magis esse liberas, neque eandem libertatis speciem omnibus competere?
latin.2134: XXXVIII. Praeterea vero quid cogit ut dicamus Deum, dum nos movet ad bona opera, a nobis auferre per gratiam suam potestatem aliter agendi, cum sine hoc constare possit gratiae divinae sua efficacia: nec desint sapientiae divinae rationes quibus praestet ut hoc agamus, idque certo ac infallibiliter, quanquam a nobis non tollat potentiam ad actum oppositum, & ad nostri etiam actus suspensionem?
latin.2135: XXXIX. Istud quoque non placet in sententia Mosis Amyraldi, quod supponit mentem atque voluntatem in omnibus suis actibus ab objectis sic determinari, ut si haec vel illa eis objiciantur, tali modo ac ratione, necessario hoc aut illud agant, neque possint aliter agere, aut ab actione cessare. Si enim potentiae rationales non minus quam brutae ad certam actionem determinentur a suis objectis, quodnam erit discrimen inter brutorum spontaneos motus, & liberas actiones creaturarum rationalium? Et quomodo dici poterunt agentia libera actuum suorum domini, & in sua potestate proprios actus habere, si objecta ipsis, non minus quam agentibus caeteris, necessitatem agendi imponant?
latin.2136: XL. Praesertim si concipiamus primo homini fuisse necessitatem impositam edendi de fructu vetito, per objecta quae, juxta Dei decretum, & divina providentia procurante & administrante, ipsi oblata fuerunt; nec Adamum potuisse ab eo abstinere, habita ratione, tum virium quas a Deo acceperat, tum incitamentorum quibus ad hoc fuit inductus, non video quae in eo fuerit culpa supplicio digna, & quomodo Deus non sit peccati ejus autor, cum esus iste illicitus necessario secutus sit ex proportione virium quas Deus ipsi indulserat, cum tentationibus & objectis variis, quae, nulla ejus culpa, sed Deo sic ordinante ac disponente, ipsi proposita sunt.
latin.2137: XLI. Denique in postrema, plurium tamen Doctorum illustrium, sententia probare non possumus, quod dicunt Deum velle ut mala fiant, licet ipso non efficiente, sed tantum permittente. Nec enim putamus Deum recte dici posse velle id quod non probat. At dici non potest mala fieri Deo approbante. Nec percipimus sensum distinctionis illius, qua distinguunt inter malum & inter mali eventum, & aiunt Deum malum quidem non velle, sed nihilominus velle mali eventum; Deumque mala ipsa nolle, sed tamen velle ut mala contingant; seu quod idem est, velle malorum existentiam quomodo potest enim existentia rei a re ipsa distingui, & qua ratione potest aliquis rem quampiam nolle, & simul velle ut res illa existat?
latin.2138: XLII. Nec minus durum est quod dicunt decreto Dei effectivo praedefinitas esse illas ipsas actiones quibus necessario malitia annexa est. Quomodo enim Deus autor peccati non erit, si aeterno suo decreto praedefinivit actum illum quo aliquis Deum ipsum odit, & nomen illius blasphemat, & juxta decretum suum, hominem in tempore ad istam actus speciem praemovet & praedeterminat?
latin.2139: XLIII. Idem absurdum videtur ex eo manifeste sequi quod dicunt malum etiam qua malum, praeordinatum esse decreto Dei, quod licet effectivum non sit, nihilominus efficax est, & tale ut, eo posito, necessario malum consequatur. Quid enim, an dicemus ex Dei decreto necesse fuisse ut primus homo in Deum rebellaret, & mandatum ab eo acceptum transgrederetur? Ac quomodo potuit juste ob peccatum puniri, cui citra ullam antecedentem culpam, imposita fuit peccandi necessitas? Et annon potius istius transgressionis culpa debet in eum refundi, a cujus decreto necessitas tam dura orta fuisse supponitur?
latin.2140: XLIV. Scio magnos illos viros qui locutionibus ejusmodi utuntur, consequentias istas non admittere, & dicta sua quantum possunt reducere ad sensum bonum atque commodum: sed quantumvis ejusmodi durae locutiones interpretatione benigna emolliantur, Christianae plebis aures non possunt non offendere, & animis audientium non injicere varios scrupulos, absque ulla necessitate. Quid enim opus mordicus adhaerere istis loquendi modis, qui nec diserte sunt in scriptura expressi, nec sunt in usu veterum Ecclesiae Doctorum?
latin.2141: XLV. At inquiet aliquis quid alienas sententias carpis? Si melius quid habes accerse, vel imperium fer. Respondeo, quaedam in hoc negotio apud me certa esse atque indubitata, alia vero a me ignorari. Ex scriptura clarum est, & ratio quoque ipsa astipulatur omnia Dei providentia regi, & ita subesse decretis divinis, ut nihil Deo inscio sive invito fiat. Quicquid bene fit, ad illum ut bonorum omnium authorem referendum esse; sed malorum omnium culpam penes creaturam solam residere. Nihil tamen mali contingere, nisi quantum Deus certo consilio sinit & non impedit; Deumque sic moderari malas hominum actiones, illisque ea ratione uti, ut inde multa bona eliciat, illasque ad varios & optimos fines dirigat.
latin.2142: XLVI. Nec minus ratione & experientia certum, & etiam scripturae authoritate confirmatum, homines seu bene, sive male agant, libertate sua uti, & ita libere moveri, ut laude vel vituperio, vel poena vel praemio merito digni habeantur, prout bene vel male egerint.
latin.2143: XLVII. Ex quibus consequitur sic agnoscendam esse libertatem humanam, ut tamen providentiae divinae nihil derogetur; & contra, vim & efficaciam providentiae Divinae sic extollendam esse, ut tamen creaturae libertas sua asseratur. Caeterum, modo salva sit creaturae rationalis in agendo libertas, & diligenter caveatur, ne creaturae culpa in Deum transferatur, quasi peccati causa vel author esset, providentiae divinae decretis & efficaciae nimium non posse tribui.
latin.2144: XLVIII. Sed sigillatim exponere quae sit decretorum divinorum ratio, & qua ratione Deus creaturas rationales sic regat & moveat, ut naturae suae congruenter, id est, libere semper agant, fateor rem esse quae captum meum superat. Non dubito quin sapientiae & potentiae divinae, quae utraque infinita est, rationes abunde suppetant quibus id praestent effectum; sed illas assequi, non puto tenuitatis esse meae. Nec enim in iis quae legi aut excogitare potui quicquam inveni quod mihi omni ex parte satisfaceret, & in quo animus, tanquam re comperta & percepta, posset acquiescere. Itaque malo ingenue ignorantiam meam hac in parte fateri, quam jactare me scire, quae ipse nescire mihi conscius sum: & aliis tanquam vera obtrudere, de quorum veritate non sum ipse plene persuasus.
latin.2145: XLIX. Nec me pudet hujus meae ignorantiae. Tuto enim ignoratur, quod nec Deus aperte in verbo suo revelavit, nec humana ratio per se investigare potest. Jam autem scriptura sacra manifeste docet quidem, omnia divina providentia regi, nec quicquam, nisi ipso consulto sinente, fieri, & ab aeterno Deo nota esse & definita omnia opera sua: modum vero quo Deus causas secundas movet, quae sit ratio decretorum illius, & qua ratione illa exequatur, & omnia ad finem destinatum perducat, scriptura sacra non aperit, nec studet humanae curiositati super eo satisfacere.
latin.2146: L. Imo satis indicat rem esse quam Deus voluit humanis ingeniis esse occultam atque imperviam, & in cujus profundum mentis nostrae acies penetrare non valet. Quo pertinet illud Dei apud Isaiam. Non enim cogitationes meae, cogitationes vestrae; neque viae vestrae viae meae. Quia sicut exaltantur coeli a terra, sic exaltatae sunt viae meae a viis vestris, & cogitationes meae a cogitationibus vestris: Item illud Apostoli in epistola ad Romanos, O Altitudo divitiarum sapientiae & scientiae Dei: quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, & investigabiles viae ejus! Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini? Aut quis consiliarius ejus fuit?
latin.2147: LI. Nec tamen propterea damno virorum Doctorum conatum, qui nituntur lucem aliquam his tenebris inferre, ac per se experiri quo possit in re tanta animus noster assurgere; modo id fiat cum debita modestia, & vera ac seria imbecillitatis nostrae agnitione: & ita sic quisque proprii ingenii conjecturas & commenta proferat, ut aliorum etiam rationes audiat, nec putet se solum sapere, acerbe & hostiliter contendens & rixans cum iis, qui se statim dictatis illius subjicere nolunt. Verum ista qualiacunque Scholae reservanda sunt, nec facile apud plebem movendae difficultates, quae eos scrupulos animis injiciunt, quos additae solutiones obscurae & infirmae discutere non valent.

sections.title: The decree covers good and evil actions; the energetic decree divided into effective and permissive
sections.pass_a: XXVI. Further they contend that not only the good actions of free causes, but also the evil, are subject to a decree of this kind: For both are done with God decreeing and willing. But that absolute and energetic decree they distinguish into an effective decree by which God determined to effect something, and into a permissive decree by which God determined to permit something. But to this effective decree of God they subject not only the good actions of creatures, but also the evil, if they be considered in themselves, and according to that which is positive in them, and as they are distinguished from the malice which denominates them. For they think these and those are done with God not only decreeing, but also stirring and moving the second causes, and applying and determining them to doing this or that. But they teach that the very malice of free actions is not effected by God, but only permitted.
pass_b: They further contend that not only the good actions of free causes but also the evil ones fall under a decree of this kind, since both are done by God's decree and will. They divide that absolute and energetic decree into an effective decree, by which God resolved to bring something about, and a permissive decree, by which God resolved to permit something.

Under God's effective decree they place not only the good actions of creatures but also the evil ones, considered in themselves, according to what is positive in them, and as distinguished from the malice that gives them their name. They think both kinds are done not only by God's decree but also by his stirring and moving the second causes, applying and determining them to do this or that.
The malice of free actions itself, however, they teach is not brought about by God but only permitted.

lemmas.latin: Utrasque enim Deo decernente & volente fieri
lemmas.gloss: For both are done with God decreeing and willing

lemmas.latin: in decretum permissivum quo Deus constituit aliquid permittere
lemmas.gloss: into a permissive decree by which God determined to permit something

lemmas.latin: a malitia quae ipsas denominat

choices.why: God's decree to permit, distinguished from the effective decree to bring about; kept as the Reformed scholastics' term.

sections.title: The permissive decree, though not effective, is efficacious; God wills that evil come about
sections.pass_a: XXVII. Yet they will that decree by which God determined to permit evil, as such, though not effective, to be nevertheless efficacious: whence it is that all things which are done, both good and evil, they attribute to the decree of God, as they call it by a Greek word, energetic, which they afterwards subdivide into effective and efficacious. For according to them, it is no less necessary that, God's permissive decree being posited, evil be done by God permitting; than, God's effective decree being posited, it is necessary that good be done by God approving and effecting. And so they insist that it can and ought truly to be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done, he himself permitting: Because, namely, the divine will is borne not only to the permission of evil, but also to the event of the evil action itself.
pass_b: Yet they hold that the decree by which God resolved to permit evil as such, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious. That is why they ascribe everything that is done, good and evil alike, to God's decree which they call, with a Greek word, 'energetic', and which they then subdivide into effective and efficacious.

On their view, once God's permissive decree is in place, it is no less necessary that evil be done with God permitting it than, once his effective decree is in place, that good be done with God approving and bringing it about.

So they insist that it can and should truly be said not only that God wills to permit evil, but also that he wills evil to be done by his permission. The reason is that the divine will is directed not only to permitting evil but also to the actual outcome of the evil action.

lemmas.latin: licet non effectivum, efficax tamen esse volunt
lemmas.gloss: though not effective, they will it to be nevertheless efficacious

lemmas.latin: ut graeca voce vocant, energetico
lemmas.gloss: as they call it by a Greek word, energetic

lemmas.latin: sed etiam in eventum ipsius actionis malae

choices.why: The Reformed scholastics' Greek-derived term for God's operative decree, divided into effective and permissive; kept as their term.

sections.title: Their defence: evil comes by God's decree but not his efficiency; the creature fails; the entity of the act is good
sections.pass_a: XXVIII. Yet they do not think it follows thence that God is the author of sin: since although evil is done with God decreeing, nevertheless it is not done with God effecting, but with the creature failing from the certain permission of God. And although what is positive in an evil action is referred to God as to the efficient cause, yet God is not on that account the cause of evil, because namely the entity of an action however evil is good, but malice formally consists in a certain privation of rectitude.
pass_b: They deny, however, that this makes God the author of sin. Evil happens as God has decreed, yet God is not the one who works it: it comes from the creature falling short, under a definite permission of God.

And although what is positive in an evil action is traced to God as its efficient cause, God is not for that reason the cause of evil. The being of an action, however evil, is good, whereas malice formally consists in a certain lack of rectitude.

lemmas.latin: sed creatura ex certa permissione Dei deficiente
lemmas.gloss: but with the creature failing from the certain permission of God

lemmas.latin: actionis quantumvis malae entitas est bona
lemmas.gloss: the entity of an action however evil is good

lemmas.gloss: consists in a certain privation of rectitude

sections.title: Objection that God authors what he wills; reply: to will a thing in itself differs from willing its outcome
sections.pass_a: XXIX. But if anyone object that God plainly seems the author of those things which he wills to be and be done, since the will of God is the cause of things, they answer that it is one thing to will a thing in itself, another to will a thing as to its event. Then that God first and properly wills not to hinder sin: and only consequently wills the event of sin: because what God does not hinder, therefore comes about because he does not hinder it.
pass_b: If someone objects that God plainly appears to be the author of what he wills to be and to be done, since God's will is the cause of things, they reply that willing a thing for its own sake is one thing and willing a thing as to its outcome is another.
They add that God first and properly wills not to hinder sin, and wills the outcome of sin only as a consequence. For what God does not hinder comes about precisely because he does not hinder it.

lemmas.latin: aliud est velle rem aliquam per se, aliud velle rem quoad eventum
lemmas.gloss: it is one thing to will a thing in itself, another to will a thing as to its event

lemmas.latin: primo & proprie vult non impedire peccatum
lemmas.gloss: first and properly wills not to hinder sin

lemmas.latin: ideo evenit quia non impedit
lemmas.gloss: therefore comes about because he does not hinder it

sections.title: Special and general will: by the general will God wills sin only because he wills it to come about
sections.pass_a: XXX. And besides they distinguish a double will of God, one general, the other special. The special will with them is that by which God at once approves and effects something. And the object of this will depends on it, and follows it as an effect its cause. By which will they teach that God wills good, and nills evil as evil, according to that, Thou art a God that willest not iniquity. But the general will in their opinion is that by which God wills something not to be, and wills also for certain causes not to forbid certain things and consequently wills them to come about, which yet he does not simply approve: or it is the decree of God by which he wills something not as to approval, and as to effecting by himself, but only as to a certain permitted effecting by others: and so, they say, the thing to be done does not depend on the will of God, but only on the will of the failing creature. And by this will they say God wills sin, as the fall of Adam for example, not indeed simply, but only because he wills it to come about.
pass_b: They also distinguish two wills in God, one general and the other special. The special will, for them, is that by which God both approves and brings about something. Its object depends on it and follows from it as an effect follows its cause. By this will, on their account, God wills what is good and is unwilling toward evil as evil, as in the verse, 'You are a God who does not will iniquity.'

The general will, on their view, is that by which God wills something not to be, and also, for definite reasons, wills not to forbid certain things and so wills them to come about, though he does not simply approve them. Or it is God's decree by which he wills something not as approving it or doing it himself, but only as a permitted doing by others.

And so, they say, the thing to be done depends not on God's will but only on the will of the failing creature. By this will, they say, God wills sin, the fall of Adam for example, not simply but only in that he wills it to come about.

lemmas.gloss: one general, the other special

choices.why: The Reformed scholastics' term for God's will that something come about by permission without approval, set against his special will; kept as their term.

sections.title: Distinctions of necessity: absolute and hypothetical; of coaction and of infallibility
sections.pass_a: XXXI. But that they may reconcile that necessity, which the decree of God imposes on any events whatever, with their contingency and freedom, they distinguish first between absolute necessity and the necessity which is from hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. But necessity from hypothesis is that by which what in itself and simply can not be, or be otherwise, yet a certain condition being posited, cannot be otherwise. Then necessity is distinguished by them into that which is of coaction, and that which is only of infallibility. Necessity of coaction is that which through a cause acting from outside brings force on things, and impels them by compulsion to do this or that. But necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing as to its event is certainly and immutably future: yet so that if we regard the cause of the thing in itself, it can either not come about, or come about otherwise. Of which necessity that axiom is to be understood, Everything that is, while it is, necessarily is.
pass_b: To reconcile the necessity that God's decree places on every event with the contingency and freedom of those events, they first distinguish absolute necessity from necessity on a hypothesis. Absolute necessity is that by which something simply cannot be otherwise. Necessity on a hypothesis is that by which something that in itself and simply can fail to be, or be otherwise, cannot be otherwise once a certain condition is given.

Next they divide necessity into the necessity of coercion and the necessity of mere infallibility. The necessity of coercion is that by which a cause acting from outside applies force to things and drives them by compulsion to do this or that.

The necessity of infallibility is that by which a thing is certainly and unchangeably going to happen, yet such that, if we look at the thing's cause in itself, it could fail to happen or happen otherwise. This is the necessity meant in the axiom, 'Everything that is, while it is, is necessarily.'

lemmas.latin: necessitatem quae est ex hypothesi
lemmas.gloss: the necessity which is from hypothesis

lemmas.latin: eam quae est tantum infallibilitatis
lemmas.gloss: that which is only of infallibility

lemmas.latin: Omne quod est, dum est, necessario est
lemmas.gloss: Everything that is, while it is, necessarily is

choices.why: Necessity that holds only given a condition, contrasted with absolute necessity; kept as the Schools' term.

sections.title: Free acts are necessary only on the decree's hypothesis and by infallibility; freedom and necessity do not clash
sections.pass_a: XXXII. These distinctions being posited, they say that the things which are done by free and contingent causes come about indeed necessarily, in respect of the divine decree, but not absolutely but only from the hypothesis of that decree; nor is that necessity of coaction but only of infallibility, because namely God foreordained that they should be done: but that this kind of necessity does not take away the freedom of second causes, but rather establishes it: since, to wit, freedom and necessity do not destroy each other, but freedom and coaction. For, they say, from the decree of God it is not only necessary that a contingent and free cause act, but also that it act contingently and freely: because God by his decree determined not only the single events of things, but also their mode and manner.
pass_b: With these distinctions in place, they say that what free and contingent causes do does indeed come about necessarily with respect to the divine decree. But it does so not absolutely, only on the hypothesis of that decree; and the necessity is not one of coercion but only of infallibility, because God foreordained that these things should be done.
This kind of necessity, they say, does not remove the freedom of second causes but rather secures it, since it is not freedom and necessity that cancel each other out but freedom and coercion.

'For,' they say, 'God's decree makes it necessary not only that a contingent and free cause act, but also that it act contingently and freely. By his decree God determined not only each event but also its mode and manner.'

lemmas.latin: solum ex decreti illius hypothesi
lemmas.gloss: only from the hypothesis of that decree

lemmas.latin: libertas & necessitas non se invicem perimunt, sed libertas & coactio
lemmas.gloss: freedom and necessity do not destroy each other, but freedom and coaction

lemmas.latin: sed etiam eorum modum & rationem
lemmas.gloss: but also their mode and manner

choices.why: Necessity that holds only given a condition, contrasted with absolute necessity; kept as the Schools' term.

sections.title: God moves free causes congruously; power to the opposite remains in the divided sense (Perkins, Twisse)
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. To which they add, that God moves free causes as is congruous and agreeable to their nature, namely by softly bending the will, and inclining it through objects shown by the intellect, and not otherwise than that man consult and deliberate with himself about what he is going to do, and choose from his own judgement what seems to him to be followed. Nay that a free cause is so determined by the decree of God, and by the motion which follows the decree, to doing this or that, that yet at the same time there remains in it the power of not acting and acting otherwise, not indeed in the composite sense but in the divided sense: because although with the divine preordination to this or that act the opposite act or cessation from the same act does not stand together, yet with it there stands together very well the power to the contrary act, or to the suspension of the act itself: Which doctrine is that of William Perkins in the little book on the mode and order of predestination, and of Twisse his vindicator, and of many other most renowned men among the Reformed, as may be seen at length in the same Twisse in the whole second book of the vindication of that Perkinsian little book.
pass_b: They add that God moves free causes in a way suited and agreeable to their nature: by gently bending the will and inclining it through objects shown to it by the intellect, and only in such a way that a man consults and deliberates with himself about what he will do, and chooses by his own judgement what seems to him the course to follow.

They say further that a free cause is so determined to do this or that by God's decree, and by the motion that follows the decree, that there still remains in it the power not to act and to act otherwise, not in the composite sense but in the divided sense.

For although the opposite act, or ceasing from that act, cannot stand together with God's preordination to this or that act, the power to the contrary act, or to suspending the act, stands with it perfectly well.

This is the teaching of William Perkins in his little book on the mode and order of predestination, of Twisse who defended him, and of many other very distinguished men among the Reformed. It can be seen at length in Twisse, throughout the second book of his defence of Perkins's little book.

lemmas.latin: voluntatem molliter flectendo
lemmas.gloss: by softly bending the will

lemmas.latin: non quidem in sensu composito sed in sensu diviso
lemmas.gloss: not indeed in the composite sense but in the divided sense

lemmas.latin: Tuissi illius vindicis
lemmas.gloss: of Twisse his vindicator

choices.why: The Schools' distinction between a proposition taken with its supposition (composite) and apart from it (divided); kept as technical terms.

notes: William Perkins (1558-1602), De praedestinationis modo et ordine (Cambridge, 1598), answered by Arminius; William Twisse (c. 1578-1646), Vindiciae gratiae, potestatis, ac providentiae Dei (Amsterdam, 1632), a defence of Perkins against Arminius.

sections.title: Le Blanc: none of these opinions satisfies; each labours under a notable difficulty
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. Further although I look up to the genius and learning of all those Doctors, yet I cannot rest in any of the said opinions. For they do not remove every scruple. Nor is there any of them which does not seem to me to labour under some notable difficulty.
pass_b: For all my respect for the talent and learning of all these doctors, I cannot rest in any of the opinions described. They do not remove every doubt, and every one of them seems to me to struggle with some serious difficulty.

sections.title: Against the middle-knowledge view: hard to reconcile with victorious, efficacious grace taught by the orthodox School
sections.pass_a: XXXV. For that opinion which builds before the divine decrees a conditional knowledge of the future inclination and propensity of the will to this or that part, if such an occasion of acting be offered it; And which establishes that God did not otherwise foreordain the actions of men, than because he willed to create them in that state, and to offer them those occasions of acting, whence he foresaw it would follow that they, by means of his general concurrence, would act in such a way, and would elicit these rather than those volitions not by some necessity, imposed either by the objects themselves, or by some action of God, but because they of themselves would so determine themselves, since the contrary was in their power: this, I say, opinion avoids indeed many inconveniences by which other opinions are pressed: but with it can hardly be reconciled the victorious and of itself efficacious grace, which subjects free choice to itself, but is by no means to be subjected to free choice, which the orthodox School proclaims.
pass_b: Take first the opinion that sets before the divine decrees a conditional knowledge of how the will would lean and incline, one way or the other, if a given occasion for acting were offered it. It holds that God foreordained men's actions only in that he willed to create them in that state and offer them those occasions for acting.

From this he foresaw that, with his general concurrence, they would act in such a way and would produce these volitions rather than those. They would do so not by any necessity laid on them by the objects themselves or by some action of God, but because they would so determine themselves of their own accord, the contrary being in their power.

This opinion, I say, does avoid many of the awkward consequences that press on the others. But it can hardly be reconciled with the grace that conquers and is efficacious of itself, which brings free choice under itself and is by no means to be made subject to free choice, as the orthodox School proclaims.

lemmas.latin: divinis decretis praestruit scientiam conditionatam
lemmas.gloss: builds before the divine decrees a conditional knowledge

lemmas.latin: mediante ipsius generali concursu
lemmas.gloss: by means of his general concurrence

lemmas.latin: gratia victrix & per se efficax
lemmas.gloss: the victorious and of itself efficacious grace

sections.title: Besides, God's absolute predefinition before the will's determination is foreseen brings an antecedent necessity
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. Add that, although God, before he decrees anything about us, foreknows what the will will do, on the hypothesis that it be placed in such circumstances, and motives of this kind come to it; yet if God foreordains something as simply future, before the absolutely foreseen determination of our will, thence is born a certain antecedent necessity, since what God predefines must altogether be: which necessity seems no less to conflict with freedom than if no such conditional knowledge had preceded, since that knowledge does not make such a decree of God to be in our power.
pass_b: Add this. Suppose that before decreeing anything about us God foreknows what the will would do on the supposition that it is placed in such circumstances and such motives are brought to bear. Still, if God foreordains something as simply going to happen before the absolute determination of our will is foreseen, an antecedent necessity arises from it, since what God predefines must without fail come to be.
This necessity seems no less at odds with freedom than if no such conditional knowledge had gone before, since that knowledge does not put such a decree of God in our power.

lemmas.latin: ex hypothesi quod constituatur in talibus circumstantiis
lemmas.gloss: on the hypothesis that it be placed in such circumstances

lemmas.latin: inde nascitur quaedam necessitas antecedens
lemmas.gloss: thence is born a certain antecedent necessity

lemmas.latin: non faciat ut tale Dei decretum sit in nostra potestate
lemmas.gloss: does not make such a decree of God to be in our power

choices.why: God's fixing an act beforehand by decree; 'predefine' keeps the Schools' term distinct from predetermination.

sections.title: Against Strang: no ground to grade deliberate acts as more or less free
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. In the opinion of John Strang that seems to me altogether improbable, that he sets up a difference as to freedom among those things which are done by men advisedly and deliberately; as though some only were free with that freedom which is placed in indifference, and by which man can act or not act; do this or that, but others only with a simple freedom for which indetermination of the will is not required, but only that man act spontaneously and with judgement. To which kind he thinks belong, not only all good actions, but also many which of their kind are neither good nor evil. For since we experience that we use our reason and judgement, and the power of choosing in the same way, not only in all the actions of civil life, but also in good ones, why shall we think some are more free than others, and that the same species of freedom does not belong to all?
pass_b: In John Strang's opinion, what seems to me quite improbable is the difference he sets up, as regards freedom, among things men do on purpose and after deliberation. As he has it, only some acts are free with the freedom that lies in indifference, by which a man can act or not act, do this or that, while others are free only with a simple freedom that does not require the will's indetermination, only that a man act willingly and with judgement.

To this second class, he thinks, belong not only all good actions but also many that in their kind are neither good nor evil. Yet we find by experience that we use our reason, judgement and power of choice in the same way, not only in all the actions of civil life but also in good ones. Why, then, should we think that some acts are freer than others, and that the same kind of freedom does not belong to them all?

lemmas.latin: discrimen quoad libertatem statuit
lemmas.gloss: he sets up a difference as to freedom

lemmas.latin: libertate simplici ad quam non requiritur voluntatis indeterminatio
lemmas.gloss: with a simple freedom for which indetermination of the will is not required

lemmas.latin: quare putabimus alias aliis magis esse liberas

sections.title: Nothing forces us to say grace removes the power to act otherwise; it can be efficacious without that
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. But besides what compels us to say that God, while he moves us to good works, takes away from us by his grace the power of acting otherwise, since without this divine grace can have its efficacy: nor are reasons of divine wisdom lacking by which it may bring it about that we do this, and that certainly and infallibly, although it does not take from us the power to the opposite act, and to the suspension also of our act?
pass_b: Besides, what forces us to say that when God moves us to good works he takes from us, by his grace, the power to act otherwise? Divine grace can have its efficacy without this.
Nor does divine wisdom lack ways to ensure that we do the good, and do it certainly and infallibly, even though it does not take from us the power to the opposite act, or even to suspend our act.

lemmas.latin: a nobis auferre per gratiam suam potestatem aliter agendi
lemmas.gloss: takes away from us by his grace the power of acting otherwise

lemmas.latin: nec desint sapientiae divinae rationes
lemmas.gloss: nor are reasons of divine wisdom lacking

lemmas.latin: ad nostri etiam actus suspensionem
lemmas.gloss: to the suspension also of our act

sections.title: Against Amyraut: if objects necessitate rational powers as brute ones, freedom differs not from brute spontaneity
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. This also does not please me in the opinion of Moses Amyraut, that he supposes the mind and will in all their acts to be so determined by objects, that if these or those be set before them, in such a mode and manner, they necessarily do this or that, nor can act otherwise, or cease from acting. For if rational powers no less than brute be determined to a certain action by their objects, what will be the difference between the spontaneous motions of brutes, and the free actions of rational creatures? And how can free agents be called masters of their acts, and have their own acts in their power, if objects impose on them, no less than on other agents, a necessity of acting?
pass_b: In Moses Amyraut's opinion, too, I am not satisfied with his assumption that in all their acts the mind and will are so determined by objects that, if these or those are set before them in a certain way and manner, they necessarily do this or that and cannot act otherwise or stop acting.

If rational powers, no less than brute ones, are determined to a given action by their objects, what difference will there be between the spontaneous motions of animals and the free actions of rational creatures?
And how can free agents be called masters of their acts and be said to have their own acts in their power, if objects impose a necessity of acting on them no less than on other agents?

lemmas.latin: ab objectis sic determinari
lemmas.gloss: to be so determined by objects

lemmas.latin: inter brutorum spontaneos motus
lemmas.gloss: between the spontaneous motions of brutes

lemmas.latin: actuum suorum domini
lemmas.gloss: masters of their acts

sections.title: Applied to Adam: if the objects God arranged necessitated his eating, where is his guilt, and how is God not author?
sections.pass_a: XL. Especially if we conceive that a necessity was imposed on the first man of eating of the forbidden fruit, through objects which, according to God's decree, and divine providence procuring and administering, were offered to him; and that Adam could not abstain from it, account being taken, both of the strength which he had received from God, and of the incitements by which he was induced to this, I do not see what fault there was in him worthy of punishment, and how God is not the author of his sin, since that unlawful eating necessarily followed from the proportion of the strength which God had granted him, with the temptations and various objects, which, through no fault of his, but God so ordaining and disposing, were proposed to him.
pass_b: This is especially so if we suppose that a necessity of eating the forbidden fruit was laid on the first man through objects offered to him according to God's decree, with divine providence arranging and managing it. Suppose too that Adam could not refrain from it, given both the strength he had received from God and the incitements by which he was led to it.

Then I do not see what fault there was in him that deserved punishment, or how God is not the author of his sin. That unlawful eating would have followed necessarily from the match between the strength God had granted him and the temptations and various objects set before him, not by any fault of his but because God so ordained and arranged it.

lemmas.latin: necessitatem impositam edendi de fructu vetito
lemmas.gloss: a necessity imposed of eating of the forbidden fruit

lemmas.latin: non video quae in eo fuerit culpa supplicio digna
lemmas.gloss: I do not see what fault there was in him worthy of punishment

lemmas.latin: nulla ejus culpa, sed Deo sic ordinante ac disponente
lemmas.gloss: through no fault of his, but God so ordaining and disposing

sections.title: Against the last view: God cannot be said to will what he does not approve; willing evil's existence is incoherent
sections.pass_a: XLI. Finally in the last opinion, yet that of many illustrious Doctors, we cannot approve that they say God wills that evils be done, though he does not effect but only permits. For we do not think God can rightly be said to will that which he does not approve. But it cannot be said that evils are done with God approving. Nor do we perceive the sense of that distinction, by which they distinguish between evil and the event of evil, and say that God indeed does not will evil, but nevertheless wills the event of evil; and that God nills evils themselves, but yet wills that evils happen; or what is the same, wills the existence of evils for how can the existence of a thing be distinguished from the thing itself, and in what way can anyone nill some thing, and at the same time will that that thing exist?
pass_b: Finally, in the last opinion, though it is held by many illustrious doctors, we cannot accept their saying that God wills evils to be done, even though he does not bring them about but only permits them. We do not think God can rightly be said to will what he does not approve, and it cannot be said that evils are done with God's approval.

Nor can we see the sense of the distinction they draw between evil and the outcome of evil, when they say that God does not will evil yet does will the outcome of evil; that God refuses evils themselves yet wills that evils should happen; or, what amounts to the same, that he wills the existence of evils.
How can the existence of a thing be distinguished from the thing itself? And how can anyone refuse something and at the same time will that it exist?

lemmas.gloss: yet that of many illustrious Doctors

lemmas.latin: Nec enim putamus Deum recte dici posse velle id quod non probat
lemmas.gloss: For we do not think God can rightly be said to will that which he does not approve

sections.title: Harder still: acts to which malice is necessarily joined, predefined by the effective decree, make God author
sections.pass_a: XLII. Nor is it less hard that they say those very actions to which malice is necessarily annexed have been predefined by the effective decree of God. For how will God not be the author of sin, if by his eternal decree he predefined that act by which someone hates God himself, and blasphemes his name, and according to his decree, premoves and predetermines man in time to that species of act?
pass_b: No less harsh is their claim that the very actions to which malice is necessarily attached were predefined by God's effective decree.

How will God not be the author of sin if by his eternal decree he predefined the act by which someone hates God himself and blasphemes his name, and in time, in line with his decree, premoves and predetermines the man to that kind of act?

sections.title: The same absurdity from an efficacious decree of evil as evil: was Adam's rebellion necessary by God's decree?
sections.pass_a: XLIII. The same absurdity seems manifestly to follow from what they say, that evil also as evil, was foreordained by a decree of God, which although it be not effective, nevertheless is efficacious, and such that, it being posited, evil necessarily follows. For what, shall we say that from God's decree it was necessary that the first man should rebel against God, and transgress the command received from him? And how could he justly be punished for sin, on whom without any antecedent fault, a necessity of sinning was imposed? And should not rather the fault of that transgression be thrown back upon him, from whose decree so hard a necessity is supposed to have arisen?
pass_b: The same absurdity seems plainly to follow from their saying that evil, even as evil, was foreordained by a decree of God which, though not effective, is nevertheless efficacious, such that once it is in place evil necessarily follows.

What then? Shall we say that God's decree made it necessary for the first man to rebel against God and break the command he had received from him? How could he justly be punished for sin if a necessity of sinning was laid on him without any prior fault?
And should not the guilt of that transgression rather be thrown back on him from whose decree so harsh a necessity is supposed to have arisen?

lemmas.latin: malum etiam qua malum, praeordinatum esse decreto Dei
lemmas.gloss: evil also as evil, was foreordained by a decree of God

lemmas.latin: citra ullam antecedentem culpam
lemmas.gloss: without any antecedent fault

lemmas.latin: culpa debet in eum refundi
lemmas.gloss: the fault ought to be thrown back upon him

sections.title: These men soften their phrases, but such harsh speech needlessly troubles the people; it is neither Scripture's nor the Fathers'
sections.pass_a: XLIV. I know those great men who use expressions of this kind do not admit these consequences, and reduce their sayings as much as they can to a good and fitting sense: but however much harsh expressions of this kind be softened by kind interpretation, they cannot but offend the ears of the Christian people, and cast various scruples into the minds of hearers, without any necessity. For what need is there to cling with the teeth to these modes of speaking, which are neither expressly stated in scripture, nor are in use among the ancient Doctors of the Church?
pass_b: I know that the great men who use expressions of this kind do not admit these consequences, and bring their statements, as far as they can, to a sound and acceptable sense.

But however much such harsh expressions are softened by charitable interpretation, they cannot fail to offend the ears of Christian people and to plant various doubts in the minds of those who hear them, and that without any need. What need is there to cling tooth and nail to ways of speaking that are neither stated outright in Scripture nor used by the ancient doctors of the Church?

lemmas.gloss: do not admit these consequences

lemmas.gloss: cannot but offend the ears of the Christian people

sections.title: What Le Blanc holds certain: all things governed by providence; good from God, guilt the creature's; evil only as God permits
sections.pass_a: XLV. But someone will say, why do you pluck at others' opinions? If you have something better, bring it, or submit to command. I answer, that certain things in this business are with me certain and undoubted, but others are unknown by me. From scripture it is clear, and reason itself also assents, that all things are ruled by God's providence, and are so subject to the divine decrees, that nothing is done without God's knowing or against his will. Whatever is well done, is to be referred to him as the author of all goods; but the guilt of all evils resides with the creature alone. Yet that nothing evil happens, except so far as God by certain counsel allows and does not hinder; and that God so moderates the evil actions of men, and uses them in that way, that he draws thence many goods, and directs them to various and excellent ends.
pass_b: Someone will say: 'Why do you pick at other men's opinions? If you have something better, bring it out, or else take orders.' I answer that in this matter some things are certain and beyond doubt for me, while others I do not know.

It is clear from Scripture, and reason itself agrees, that all things are governed by God's providence and are so subject to the divine decrees that nothing happens without God's knowledge or against his will. Whatever is done well is to be credited to him as the author of all good things, while the guilt of all evils lies with the creature alone.

Yet nothing evil happens except so far as God, by a settled plan, allows it and does not hinder it. And God so governs men's evil actions, and uses them in such a way, that he draws many good things from them and directs them to various excellent ends.

sections.title: Equally certain: men use their freedom, and are rightly praised or blamed, rewarded or punished
sections.pass_a: XLVI. Nor is it less certain by reason and experience, and also confirmed by the authority of scripture, that men whether they act well, or ill, use their freedom, and are so freely moved, that they are deservedly held worthy of praise or blame, or punishment or reward, according as they have acted well or ill.
pass_b: It is no less certain by reason and experience, and confirmed also by the authority of Scripture, that men use their freedom whether they act well or badly. They are moved so freely that they are rightly held to deserve praise or blame, punishment or reward, according as they have acted well or badly.

lemmas.gloss: use their freedom

lemmas.gloss: are so freely moved

sections.title: Hence both are to be held together; providence cannot be overstated so long as freedom is safe and God not made author of sin
sections.pass_a: XLVII. From which it follows that human freedom is so to be acknowledged, that yet nothing be derogated from divine providence; and on the contrary, that the force and efficacy of divine Providence is so to be extolled, that yet its freedom be asserted to the creature. But, provided the freedom of the rational creature in acting be safe, and care be diligently taken, lest the fault of the creature be transferred to God, as though he were the cause or author of sin, too much cannot be attributed to the decrees and efficacy of divine providence.
pass_b: It follows that human freedom must be acknowledged in a way that takes nothing away from divine providence, and that the power and efficacy of divine providence must be exalted in a way that still affirms the creature's freedom.

But provided the rational creature's freedom in acting is kept intact, and great care is taken not to shift the creature's guilt onto God, as if he were the cause or author of sin, one cannot ascribe too much to the decrees and efficacy of divine providence.

sections.title: How God governs rational creatures so that they always act freely exceeds Le Blanc's grasp; he confesses ignorance
sections.pass_a: XLVIII. But to set forth in detail what is the nature of the divine decrees, and in what way God so rules and moves rational creatures, that they always act congruently to their nature, that is, freely, I confess is a matter which exceeds my grasp. I do not doubt that to divine wisdom and power, each of which is infinite, ways abundantly suffice by which they may accomplish this effect; but to attain them, I do not think belongs to my slenderness. For in those things which I have been able to read or think out I have found nothing which satisfied me on every side, and in which the mind, as in a thing found out and perceived, could rest. And so I prefer frankly to confess my ignorance in this part, than to boast that I know, things which I am conscious to myself I do not know: and to thrust on others as true, things of whose truth I am not myself fully persuaded.
pass_b: But to explain point by point the nature of the divine decrees, and how God so governs and moves rational creatures that they always act in keeping with their nature, that is, freely, is, I confess, beyond my understanding.

I do not doubt that divine wisdom and power, both of them infinite, have ample means of achieving this. But I do not think it lies within my small capacity to grasp them. In all I have been able to read or think out, I have found nothing that satisfied me on every side, nothing in which the mind could rest as in something found out and understood.
So I would rather frankly confess my ignorance on this point than boast that I know what I am aware I do not know, or press on others as true things whose truth I am not fully convinced of myself.

sections.title: No shame in ignorance where Scripture is silent: it teaches that God rules all, not the mode
sections.pass_a: XLIX. Nor am I ashamed of this my ignorance. For that is safely not known, which neither God has openly revealed in his word, nor human reason can investigate by itself. But now sacred scripture plainly teaches indeed, that all things are ruled by divine providence, and that nothing is done, except he advisedly allowing it, and that from eternity all his works are known and defined to God: but the mode by which God moves second causes, what is the nature of his decrees, and in what way he executes them, and leads all things to the destined end, sacred scripture does not open, nor is it eager to satisfy human curiosity about it.
pass_b: I am not ashamed of this ignorance of mine. It is safe not to know what God has not openly revealed in his word and what human reason cannot search out by itself.

Holy Scripture does plainly teach that all things are governed by divine providence, that nothing happens unless he deliberately allows it, and that all his works are known to God and settled from eternity.

But how God moves second causes, what the nature of his decrees is, how he carries them out and brings all things to their appointed end, Holy Scripture does not disclose, nor does it seek to satisfy human curiosity on the point.

sections.title: Scripture rather shows it hidden: Isaiah 55:8-9 and Romans 11:33-34
sections.pass_a: L. Nay it sufficiently indicates that it is a matter which God willed to be hidden and impassable to human wits, and into whose depth the edge of our mind cannot penetrate. To which pertains that word of God in Isaiah. For my thoughts are not your thoughts; nor your ways my ways. Because as the heavens are exalted from the earth, so are my ways exalted from your ways, and my thoughts from your thoughts: Likewise that of the Apostle in the epistle to the Romans, O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God: how incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who was his counsellor?
pass_b: Indeed, it shows clearly enough that this is something God willed to be hidden from human minds and closed to them, a depth our mind's sharpest sight cannot reach.

This is what God says in Isaiah: 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so are my ways high above your ways and my thoughts above your thoughts.'

So too the Apostle in the letter to the Romans: 'O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?'

sections.title: Learned attempts are not condemned if modest and charitable; but keep such questions in the School, not before the people
sections.pass_a: LI. Nor yet on that account do I condemn the endeavour of learned men, who strive to bring some light into these darknesses, and to try by themselves how far our mind can rise in so great a matter; provided it be done with due modesty, and true and serious acknowledgement of our weakness: and so let each bring forward the conjectures and devices of his own wit, that he also hear the reasons of others, nor think himself alone wise, bitterly and hostilely contending and quarrelling with those, who are unwilling straightway to submit themselves to his dictates. But these things, whatever they are, are to be reserved for the School, nor are difficulties easily to be moved among the people, which cast into minds those scruples, which added solutions obscure and weak are not able to dispel.
pass_b: Not that I therefore condemn the efforts of learned men who try to bring some light into this darkness and to test for themselves how high our mind can rise in so great a matter, provided it is done with proper modesty and a true and serious recognition of our weakness.

Let each put forward the conjectures and inventions of his own mind in such a way that he also listens to the reasoning of others. Let him not think he alone is wise, nor fight and quarrel bitterly and with hostility against those who will not at once submit to his pronouncements.

But such things, whatever they are worth, should be kept for the School. Difficulties should not lightly be raised among the people, for they plant doubts in men's minds that the obscure and weak solutions offered with them cannot clear away.
